Urban Design in the UAE and London: a market snapshot

Urban design in the UAE and London is steadier than the headlines suggest.
2026 has tested confidence in both markets. But look past sentiment to where policy and public investment are heading, and the case for urban design is getting stronger, not weaker.

The snapshot
Both markets have moved from rapid expansion to selective growth. UAE hiring dipped when the regional conflict began, then recovered within months. In London the outlook is stable, with larger multidisciplinary practices the most confident. Employers are still hiring, but they are hiring with intent.

What the research shows
• The UAE kept committing through the uncertainty. Dubai approved its Metro Gold Line and awarded the first Dubai Walk contract, in historic Al Ras, while the conflict was unfolding. Both are long-term bets on transit-led, walkable, shaded streets.
• Dubai is redesigning around people, not cars. From the 20 minute city policy to the pedestrian first spine planned for the expanded Dubai Design District, briefs are increasingly about heat, comfort and street life. That is urban design at its core.
• London is planning to grow within its own fabric. The Draft London Plan leans on brownfield land, town centres and small sites, with design codes and urban greening doing more of the work. Intensifying a city well demands more design skill, not less.
• The public sector wants more design capacity. City Hall's new framework makes it easier for public bodies to appoint design expertise, including smaller practices, and evidence on the UK's new towns has repeatedly called for stronger design review and in-house capability.
• Early-career talent needs protecting. RIBA research shows most practitioners expect AI to make it harder for juniors to learn the craft. Practices that keep investing in graduates will be the ones developing the next generation of leaders.

What this means for practices
The firms winning work now can show delivery, not just vision. Experienced masterplanners who can lead bids and carry schemes through every stage remain hard to find, and a quieter market is often the best moment to secure them.

What this means for urban designers
Climate, transit and public realm expertise travels well between London and the Gulf. Accreditation, delivery experience and a clear grasp of how policy shapes place will set the strongest candidates apart.

Urban design is a long game. Masterplans outlive market cycles, and cities will keep needing the people who shape them.

Two months back from maternity leave, after a year away from recruitment. The biggest change? AI. 🤖
 
A year ago, AI was something clients were experimenting with. Now it's in almost every conversation I have. Here's what's changed while I was away:
 
1️⃣ Nearly every company is now an AI company
AI used to be a side project for the innovation team. Now it's on every roadmap, from banks and retailers to healthcare businesses with no in-house tech team at all. Demand for AI engineers has rocketed, with UK AI Engineer job ads up 74% for perm and 96% for temp/contract roles in a year.
 
2️⃣ Job specs have changed
Almost every engineering spec I see now mentions LLMs, RAG or AI agents.
 
3️⃣ The cloud conversation has shifted
The question isn't just "AWS or Azure?" anymore. Google Cloud is the fastest-growing platform, largely because of its AI tools, and I'm recruiting for more GCP roles than ever.
 
4️⃣ Candidates use AI too
CVs and applications are more polished than ever, so the human conversation matters more. Understanding how someone thinks, and what they've really built, is where a good recruiter adds value.
 
5️⃣ It's changed how I work
I use AI to research markets, find which companies are hiring, and draft first versions. That gives me more time for the bit that matters most: talking to people.
 
The tools have changed, but recruitment is still about people and trust.
 
It's great to be back! If you're hiring AI, data or engineering talent, or you're a contractor looking for your next role, I'd love to catch up. 👋

Some of the AI risk on your rent roll sits with tenants who will never decide to use AI.

Take an outsourcer on a large, high-density floor, on a lease sized to a single contract. Its client moves the work to an AI-native provider. The contract goes, and the floor goes with it. The covenant you underwrote belonged to a business whose fate was set by someone else's procurement decision.

That is credit risk arriving all at once, rather than seats drifting down at each lease event.

It is one of three ways AI reaches an occupier, on the model in Alex Imas, Andrew Koh and Shane Legg's paper 'Organizing Intelligence'. 

Three things set the pace: 
- how well AI matches a firm's core tasks
- how much the work depends on teams
- and how deep the market is.

Adjustment is gradual and already under way. The mix changes: graduate hiring and the middle layers shrink, and seniors carry more weight. India's five largest IT services firms added a combined net 17 employees in the first nine months of FY26. In the building, it shows up as fewer seats and higher specification at lease events.

Replacement is sudden. In deep markets for bounded work, an AI-heavy competitor undercuts the incumbent and the incumbent's market disappears. Claims processing, payroll, contact centres and residential conveyancing look next.

Concentration comes once AI can run the coordination itself. Deep, fully digital markets consolidate into a few firms. Software first.

The occupier base may polarise as a result: a handful of large consolidators, and many small specialist firms. The dedicated mid-sized floor is the requirement I'd watch most closely.

None of this will show up first in a benchmark. It shows up in graduate intake, revenue per head, and requests for breaks and seat-density studies.

The document sets out the three mechanisms, five firm shapes, the red zone, and three questions to ask of every tenant.

Which names on your rent roll occupy a floor sized to someone else's contract?

Upwork Lost 10% of Its Clients. Its Take Rate Hit 20%. Guess Who Paid for the Difference.

Upwork reported Q3 on Monday. The stock jumped. Earnings beat.
But one number in the release tells a different story.
Active clients fell 10% - from 794,000 to 717,000.

And the marketplace take rate rose to 20.0% - up 110 basis points year-over-year, and up from 19.0% just three quarters ago.

Read those two lines together.

Fewer clients. Higher cut from every contract.

Where did the money come from?
1. GSV per client hit a record $5,418 - up 8% year-over-year, the ninth straight quarter of growth.
2. Connects revenue through the MCP server reached a $3 million annual run rate - a few months after launch.
3. Freelancer Plus subscription revenue grew 25% year-over-year.
4. AI-skilled talent GSV grew 55% to $112 million.

The platform is growing by monetising the freelancers who stayed - while the client base shrinks.

And then there's Upwork Now.
Also launched Monday. Clients can see available freelancers and hire in minutes - including from inside ChatGPT or Claude, without opening Upwork at all.
In early testing, clients hired in under 30 minutes - fastest under 10. Freelancer responses came in about five minutes.

That changes what "available" means. Speed is now the product.

What this means for freelancers this week:
1. A 20% take rate plus a 0–15% service fee plus Connects plus withdrawal fees is not a rate. It's a math problem. Recalculate your true net before you quote.
2. Turn on "Work Now." Availability is becoming a ranking signal. If you're not in the live feed, you're not in the fastest-growing hiring channel.
3. Stop chasing ghost jobs. Clients face zero penalty for posting and disappearing. At $0.15 per Connect and up to 16–20 Connects per bid, a dead job costs you up to $3 before you've spoken to anyone.
4. Position for AI-skilled work. That's the only category growing fast enough to offset the client decline.

The uncomfortable truth: Upwork isn't dying. It's getting more profitable by charging the supply side more - while the demand side shrinks. That's not a partnership. That's a squeeze.

Are you seeing faster hires this week - or just faster rejections?

When a major tech buyer trims internal AI budgets, it’s a reminder: experimentation without clear ROI becomes cost, not capability. Leaders must force clarity on which AI efforts deliver measurable business value.

What happened
TechCrunch reports Apple is reportedly cutting budgets for its internal AI usage, scaling back some experimental projects and internal compute spend. The story cites sources inside the company; details and full scope were not independently confirmed.

The coverage suggests growing internal scrutiny of AI spend — particularly costly compute, tooling, and staff allocated to exploratory work rather than productized features.

🔎 Why it matters:
• Intellectual property: Stalled experiments risk leaving useful IP as unproductized artifacts with limited business value.
• Business/security risk: Rapid reprioritization can create vendor, compliance, or staffing mismatches if contracts and access controls aren’t adjusted.
• Operational/strategic impact: Compute and hiring plans must align to product roadmaps or organizations will face unpredictable costs and slower time-to-market.

💡 3 practical takeaways:
1️⃣ Tie every AI project to a clear business metric, timeline, and kill-switch; review quarterly.
2️⃣ Build vendor and hiring flexibility—short-term contractors, modular contracts, and cloud commitments with scale-down options.
3️⃣ Centralize compute and cost reporting; model cost-per-feature and include infrastructure in ROI calculations.

🎯 My take:
This is discipline over optics — a push to convert exploration into accountable value. Teams that quantify impact and design flexibility will win.

I think we're asking AI to find the wrong companies.

Here's what I mean.

Say you give Clay a list of 5,000 companies and ask AI to identify which ones are most likely to need your product.

You give it your ICP, a few buying signals, and some scoring criteria.

It researches the accounts and gives you 500 high-priority companies.

Looks pretty useful.

But here's what I've been thinking about.

Where did those scoring criteria come from?

Usually, they're based on what we think makes someone a good customer.

We assume companies hiring aggressively have a certain problem. 
Or that companies using a particular technology are more likely to buy.

Sometimes we're right. 
Sometimes we're just making assumptions at scale.

I came across an interesting approach recently.

Take 20–30 customers who actually bought. 

Go through their sales conversations and figure out what was happening in their business before they started evaluating your product.

Then use AI to research what information was publicly available at that time.

Maybe they had won a large contract, opened a new office, or were dealing with a regulatory change.

Now you can look for those same situations across other companies.

I think this could completely change how we approach account research in GTM.

Because right now, we're getting really good at finding companies that match our assumptions.

I think we should spend more time understanding why our existing customers bought before deciding who to target next.

Curious if anyone's actually used past customer data to find new accounts. 

How did it work?

Most UK founders have heard of ARIA. Far fewer know about SPRIND, Germany’s Federal Agency for Breakthrough Innovation. It’s been running for longer, and its challenges are open to teams from across Europe.

There are two ways in.

The first is Challenges. These are competitions built around a single, ambitious goal. An expert jury selects the teams, which are then funded through staged, fixed-price contracts, with the field narrowed at each stage. Because SPRIND uses pre-commercial procurement rather than grants, money can arrive within days of selection, and coaching and introductions come alongside it.

Three are open now:

- Measuring with Entanglement, closing 9 November: quantum sensors that beat classical limits in real-world use. Up to about €3.3m per team across three stages, starting with up to 10 teams.
- Engineering Microbial Consortia, closing 16 November: AI-controlled microbial communities for circular biomanufacturing. Up to €4.3m per team over 38 months.
- AI-Native Chip Design, closing 30 November: using AI to compress chip design from years to weeks, run with the Dutch agency NADI. Up to €9.6m per team over 20 months, with follow-on funding in the tens of millions planned for the strongest teams.

The second is an open project proposal, which you can submit at any time. There are no funding guidelines and no standard programme. If SPRIND sees a genuine breakthrough, they build a structure around it. That might be a validation study, an R&D grant, equity or a convertible loan, plus help with hiring and business services. It’s selective: of around 2,500 ideas submitted by the end of 2025, fewer than 10% were taken forward, and decisions take about twelve weeks.

The bar is the important part. SPRIND wants innovation that replaces an existing technology or business model, not one that improves it. If your pitch is a better version of something that already exists, this isn’t the route.

Each challenge sets its own terms, so read the call documents closely. Some expect teams to be incorporated early on and to pitch in person in Leipzig.

I write my resume with AI and I deliberately keep my skills and experience vague on purpose. Why? Because in a world where we  now have little control over our intellectual property online, I refuse to contribute anything original publicly.

Some less than reputable agencies also clone resumes. They take your specific project descriptions, your metrics, your phrasing, strip your name, and submit it as a different candidate. Or they use it to pad someone else's profile. But this isn’t a new practice.

So I write at a level of specificity that's compelling to a human but useless to a copy/paste.

Specific enough to be impressive:
"Delivers $3M over 3 years on standard enterprise contracts" 
Not specific enough to be liftable:
* No system names
* No internal tooling
* No team size or org structure
* No client or product names
* No exact timeline

A hiring manager who's done 200 interviews can read the signal. A recruiter building a "super resume" for their preferred candidate can't.

The rule: if your bullet could be dropped onto another person's resume and still read as true, it's specific enough to be cloned.

As for interviews, giving generic answers or leaving out key details/changing a detail helps protect you from identity theft which has been a well documented and growing concern by the FTC in recent years. For someone like me, these things are top of mind.

So how do you protect yourself?

Locking your SSN, freezing your credit and filing relevant reports via identitytheft.gov, IC3, etc. Is a good first step. Having your documentation sorted, old and new. Any expired government issued ID is still proof of identity. If you’re working with recruiters via RTRs or third party companies, feel free to follow up with the recruiter handling the role at the actual company being presented responsible for correspondence with the RTR company. Ask for an in person meeting even if you’re just dropping in to show your face and confirm. If you’re aware of voice spoofing and how prevalent it’s become, this is a vital step.

As for overseas, protections exist in the US but the gaps are real. A credit freeze protects you in the US. It does nothing if someone in across the globe opens a bank account with your name or other info. Keeping your social media profiles with time stamps open, actually helps you in these instances. 

I also sing for fun. Protecting your voice is another hurdle altogether. So while it’s very difficult for someone to impersonate me effectively in person, the reality is, our laws, policies and tools for the individual to protect themselves haven’t caught up to where they need to be just yet. Until then, if I can’t control it, I’ll let any AI scrapers harvest AI content instead.

Curious how others are feeling as frustrated as I’ve been about this topic right now.

AI made software cheaper to build. It didn't make building a business any easier.

While everyone seems to be talking about replacing employees with AI agents and building one-person companies, I'm sitting here dreaming about having an actual team of humans.
And the funny thing is, I probably wouldn't have a business at all without AI.

A little over two years ago, when I started building Flaita com, I remember the development estimates I was getting. Hiring a team to build a platform for marketing analytics, automation, and business tools would have required money I simply didn't have.

And spending that kind of money before validating the product with real customers? That would have been a pretty questionable business decision.

Today, things are different.

AI has dramatically lowered the barrier to building software. You can turn an idea into a working MVP without raising hundreds of thousands of dollars or spending months assembling a development team.

For someone like me, coming from marketing, analytics, and entrepreneurship rather than 15 years of professional software engineering, that's an incredible opportunity.

And I took it.

Two years later, Flaita is a real platform with more than 200 active users, including large online schools on annual Enterprise plans.

Yesterday, we hit 14 new registrations in a single day. A new record for us. And another large school signed a six-month Enterprise contract. Pretty good news, actually.

Except there's another side to all of this.

I'm still the person maintaining the infrastructure, watching logs, investigating bugs, monitoring server loads, expanding resources, shipping features, dealing with technical debt, supporting customers, and trying to figure out what to build next.

With AI agents helping me through much of it.

And broooo...

There's a point where being a solo founder stops feeling like an impressive demonstration of efficiency and starts feeling like you've accidentally become an entire IT department.

I can spend a whole day solving infrastructure problems, fixing something in production, and reviewing code generated by agents. By the end of that day, the platform is running better. Maybe I've even shipped something useful.

But I've barely touched marketing, partnerships, sales, or business development. You know, the things I actually started this company to do. And that's where the whole one-person-company narrative starts to feel a little strange to me.

AI agents are fantastic. I use them constantly, and I have no intention of stopping. They can dramatically increase what a single person is capable of building.

But they don't automatically take responsibility for the business.

They don't become an experienced engineer who understands the architecture, questions a bad technical decision, and takes ownership of keeping the platform reliable.

They don't become a product partner who challenges my assumptions about what customers actually need.

And they certainly don't make the financial pressure of running a company disappear.

I don't want to replace people with agents.

I want to work with people who are better than me at what they do, who can use AI to move faster, and who can help build something none of us could build as effectively alone.

I'd love to have an experienced developer taking ownership of the technical side of Flaita. Someone who can look at the codebase and understand what's happening without needing an AI agent to explain every corner of it.

I'd love to have someone focused on product marketing, customer experience, and eventually building out entire product directions.

And someone making sure our customers, especially Enterprise clients, get the attention and support they deserve.

Not because I believe every company needs a big team. But because I don't think doing everything myself is the best way to grow this particular business anymore.

Meanwhile, the job market in tech and marketing has become something of a Hunger Games situation. At least that's how it looks from many of the conversations I've had with people in both fields. I know talented specialists who are having a genuinely difficult time finding good opportunities.

And here I am, talking to people I'd genuinely love to have on my team, knowing exactly how much they could contribute. But I can't responsibly hire them yet.

Because here's the catch.

Flaita is growing. We have paying customers, Enterprise contracts, and new users arriving from different countries. But growth and financial sustainability are two very different things.

We still don't have the stable recurring revenue needed to confidently cover an experienced developer's salary, the company's operating costs, and even a modest income for me.

Not to mention the financial obligations that have accumulated over these years of bootstrapping.

And that's the ridiculous loop I've found myself in.

To grow the business faster, I need to spend more time on customers, distribution, partnerships, and sales.

To spend more time on those things, I need to delegate a significant part of the technical work.

To delegate that work, I need money.

And to generate that money consistently, I need more time to grow the business.

Beautiful, isn't it?

Of course, investment is another possible path. But a growing user base and a few Enterprise contracts don't automatically prove that you've built a predictable, scalable business model. There's still a lot to figure out before I can confidently make that case to someone putting their money into the company.

So for now, I'm somewhere between a working SaaS business and the company I actually want to build.

And I think this is the part of the AI revolution that gets overlooked.

We've made it dramatically easier for individuals to create software. That's an incredible achievement.

But building a sustainable business still means finding customers, earning their trust, making difficult decisions, managing money, taking responsibility, and sometimes knowing when you shouldn't be doing everything yourself anymore.

AI has helped me get much further than I could have imagined two years ago.

Now I want to reach the point where I can stop being the entire team. Not because AI has failed me. But because the whole point of building a company, at least for me, was never to spend the rest of my life running it alone.

/ Mosaz

HIRING — Radiation Safety Officer | Remote | $65–$75/task

Mercor is assembling radiological safety experts to red-team frontier AI models — testing whether a model correctly judges misuse potential: answering legitimate questions fully while refusing genuinely dangerous ones.

Work: Write single-turn prompts in your domain, labelled benign / dual-use / adversarial · evaluate responses against a policy standard · write the reference answer with technical reasoning.

Why it's hard: The same isotope underpins cancer therapy and industrial radiography; the same shielding calc protects a worker and conceals a source. A model that refuses a routine dose question fails as badly as one that answers what it shouldn't.
Need — people who held the licence, not just worked under it (ideally with red-teaming experience):
Named RSO on a broad-scope licence — programme management, source inventory, compliance
RSO/deputy RSO at a university, hospital, or research institute — mixed radionuclide and sealed-source programmes
Industrial or irradiator RSO — Category 1 & 2 sealed sources, radiography, gauging, sterilisation
Licensing & compliance specialist — NRC, Agreement State, or national regulator submissions, amendments, inspections
Radiation protection manager — ALARA, audits, training, incident reporting across authorised users

Also: writing-intensive — every judgment needs a rationale a non-specialist can follow. Prior technical writing, published research, or expert witness experience is a strong signal — include a sample or link. You can pause or step away at any point without penalty.

⚠️ Unclassified only — no classified, export-controlled, NDA, or prepublication-review material. If you hold such obligations, say so and they'll scope accordingly.

The work: Write challenging single-turn prompts in your domain, labelled benign, dual-use, and adversarial · evaluate responses against a defined policy standard and judge whether each was handled correctly · write the reference answer — what a correct response looks like, and the technical reasoning for why.

The hard part is calibration, not difficulty. A benign prompt that a model wrongly refuses is as valuable as an adversarial one it wrongly answers. In chemistry, the line sits between mechanism and procedure — only someone who has run the reaction knows exactly where it falls.

Chemical Defense Researcher (USAMRICD, DoD, CDC) — toxicological agents and medical countermeasures
Synthetic / Process Chemist — route design, reaction engineering, scale-up
Analytical Chemist — detection and identification of hazardous compounds
Industrial Hygienist / Process Safety Engineer — exposure assessment, toxic release, process hazard analysis
Forensic / Toxicological Chemist — controlled substances, precursor identification, casework
Beyond technical depth: Writing-intensive. Every judgment needs a rationale a non-specialist can follow. Prior technical writing, published research, or expert witness experience is a strong signal — include a sample or link. AI red-teaming experience a plus, not required.

⚠️ Eligibility: Your work must not draw on classified or export-controlled information, or anything under NDA/prepublication review. If you hold such obligations, state it in your application and they'll scope accordingly.

Only 24% of women in Pakistan participate in the labour force. Globally, women hold just 30.5% of managerial positions.
These numbers tell us that we still have a long way to go when it comes to women's economic participation and leadership. And that is exactly why it is important to recognise and celebrate those who are already taking steps to make a difference.
Last night, I had the opportunity to attend the first-ever Pakistan National Women's Empowerment Principles (WEPs) Awards at Mohatta Palace.
It was encouraging to see organisations recognised for their efforts across leadership, workplace equality, marketing, procurement, community engagement, technology and AI, and support for SMEs.
I was also happy to see Nishat Fatima, CEO of South Air Pakistan and the first woman to lead an airline in Pakistan, among the women breaking barriers in leadership.
Having spent more than 10 years working on women's economic empowerment, training women and supporting them in starting and growing businesses, one thing I have learned is that training alone is not enough.
A woman can learn a skill and start a business, but does she have access to a market? Can she secure a contract? Will a company consider her business as a supplier?
This is why the procurement category particularly caught my attention.
When a company buys from a women-owned business, it gives that woman a customer, generates income and creates an opportunity for her business to grow.
For companies and business leaders, I believe we need to start asking three simple questions:
 
Who are we hiring?
Who are we promoting into leadership positions?
Who are we buying from?
 
More than 100 organisations in Pakistan have signed the Women's Empowerment Principles. This is encouraging, but commitments need to translate into everyday business decisions.
An award is nice. But a woman getting her first job, receiving a promotion or securing her first major business contract is even better.
Thank you to UN Women Pakistan and Ms. Fahmida Khan for this platform to recognise these efforts and encourage more organisations to take action.
Because women's empowerment cannot remain a commitment on paper. It needs to become part of how businesses operate.
 
Thank you Zarqa Khan for inviting me to be part of it.

📍 Remote
💼 Experience requirement — 5+
Build targeting agents and workflow services for the sales funnel on Microsoft Foundry, with Salesforce as the system of record.

Production Python and FastAPI
Azure OpenAI / Foundry Agent Service
Microsoft Agent Framework or equivalent
Microsoft Graph on-behalf-of (OBO) and Entra

🚀 WE ARE HIRING | AI / AGENT ENGINEER – SALES TARGETING & WORKFLOW

AARNIKSHA SOLUTIONS is looking for an experienced AI / Agent Engineer to build intelligent sales-targeting agents and workflow services using Microsoft Azure AI technologies.

📌 Position: AI / Agent Engineer – Sales Targeting & Workflow
💼 Experience: 5+ Years
🌍 Location: Remote
💰 Budget: Open 
⏳ Engagement: Contract

🔹 Key Responsibilities:

- Build and deploy AI targeting agents using Microsoft Foundry Agent Service.
- Develop nightly targeting workflows with constraint-based selection and explainable recommendations.
- Implement configurable scoring systems and ML-based ranking using LightGBM.
- Develop backend APIs using Python and FastAPI.
- Integrate Microsoft Graph APIs for Outlook mailbox monitoring, email drafts and Teams SSO.
- Build Salesforce integrations for data retrieval and idempotent write-back.
- Implement structured LLM outputs, prompt versioning, validations, evaluations and tracing.
- Collaborate with Data Engineers to define feature contracts, testing and CI/CD pipelines.

🔹 Mandatory Skills:

- Strong production experience with Python and FastAPI.
- Azure OpenAI / Microsoft Foundry Agent Service.
- Microsoft Agent Framework or equivalent agent development framework.
- Microsoft Graph API – On-Behalf-Of (OBO) authentication.
- Microsoft Entra ID and application registration.
- Hands-on experience with at least one deployed Salesforce integration.
- Practical experience in Ranking ML and LightGBM.
- Experience building and deploying production-grade AI agent solutions.

🔹 Good to Have:

- Teams Toolkit and Microsoft Teams integration.
- Azure Container Apps and Service Bus.
- Azure SQL / Cosmos DB.
- Bicep and GitHub Actions.
- AI-assisted development practices.

⚠️ Important: Candidates with only Copilot Studio, prompt engineering, governance or analytics-enablement experience will not be considered.
